source.name: Harvard University CS50 — Introduction to Computer Science

course.title: CS50: Computer Science & Problem Solving
course.description: A first course in computer science: how machines represent information, how to write and reason about programs in C and Python, the algorithms and data structures underneath them, and how to store data and put an app on the web. Structure adapted from Harvard University's CS50 Introduction to Computer Science (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0); all explanations original.

questions.prompt: The binary number 1011 equals which decimal value?
questions.explanation: 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = 11 — see 'Computational thinking and representing information'.

questions.prompt: What does a compiler do?
options: runs a program line by line as text
translates source code into machine code before it runs
questions.explanation: A compiler such as clang turns C source into an executable of machine instructions ahead of time.

questions.prompt: Binary search requires that the data first be…
questions.explanation: Binary search only works on sorted data because it discards half the range each step.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many steps does binary search take on a sorted list of n items?
questions.explanation: Halving the search space each step gives about log2(n) comparisons — that is O(log n).

questions.prompt: In C, what does malloc do?
options: requests a block of memory on the heap at run time
questions.explanation: malloc allocates heap memory and returns a pointer to it; you later release it with free.

questions.prompt: A hash table aims to give lookups that are on average…
questions.explanation: A good hash function spreads keys across buckets so a lookup is roughly constant time.

questions.prompt: Which SQL statement reads rows from a table?
questions.explanation: SELECT retrieves rows; the others add, change, or remove them.

questions.prompt: In web terms, what does HTTP status code 404 mean?
questions.explanation: 404 means the requested resource was not found on the server.

lessons.title: Computational thinking and representing information
lessons.grammar_note: A bit is a single 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits and can hold 256 different values (0 to 255).

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Convert between binary and decimal, explain how text and other data become numbers, and describe computing as turning inputs into outputs through precise steps. Warm-up: from the diagnostic, what decimal value does binary 1011 stand for?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A computer stores everything as bits — 0s and 1s — because a physical switch is easily either off or on. Binary is just base 2: each position is a power of two, so the bits ...8 4 2 1 combine to make any whole number. Text is represented by agreeing on a code that maps characters to numbers. ASCII uses one byte per character, so 'A' is 65 and 'a' is 97. ASCII only covers 128 core characters, so Unicode extends the idea to cover every writing system and even emoji, commonly encoded as UTF-8. Images, sound, and video are numbers too: a pixel is a trio of red, green, and blue values, each 0 to 255. Computing, at its core, is taking an input, applying an algorithm — a precise sequence of steps — and producing an output.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Binary to decimal: 1011 = 1*8 + 0*4 + 1*2 + 1*1 = 11. Decimal to binary: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1 = 1101. Counting: with 8 bits you can represent 2^8 = 256 values, 0 through 255. Text: the string 'HI' is the code points 72 and 73 in ASCII. Color: the RGB triple (255, 0, 0) is pure red, since red is maxed and green and blue are zero. Notice a pattern: adding one bit doubles how many values you can store, which is exactly why binary counting grows so fast.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Convert binary 100 to decimal. 2) Convert decimal 10 to binary. 3) How many distinct values fit in 4 bits? 4) In ASCII 'A' is 65; what number is 'C'? 5) What color is the RGB triple (0, 0, 0)? Answers: 1) 1*4 = 4. 2) 8 + 2 = 1010. 3) 2^4 = 16. 4) 65 + 2 = 67. 5) black — all three channels are zero.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading binary positions as powers of ten instead of powers of two. Mistake: assuming ASCII can encode any language — it cannot, which is why Unicode exists. Exit: (a) What is binary 1111 in decimal? (b) How many values does one byte hold? Answers: 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 15; 256.

lessons.title: C and the anatomy of a program
lessons.grammar_note: In C every statement ends with a semicolon, and a variable must be declared with a type such as int, char, or float before use.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Read a small C program, name its parts, and describe the journey from source code to a running executable. Warm-up: what step turns human-readable C into instructions the processor can execute?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: C is a compiled language: you write source code in a text file, then a compiler such as clang translates the whole file into machine code, producing an executable you run. A minimal C program has a main function, which is where execution begins. You include libraries with #include to borrow ready-made functions, declare variables with explicit types, and control flow with conditions and loops. Because C is close to the machine, it makes the costs of memory and speed visible — which is exactly why it is a good place to learn what a program really is before moving to friendlier languages.

sections.heading: Worked examples
Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which function is a C program's entry point? 2) What does \n produce in printf? 3) In 'for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)', how many times does the body run? 4) Why must you write #include <stdio.h> to use printf? 5) What punctuation ends a C statement? Answers: 1) main. 2) a newline. 3) five times, for i = 0,1,2,3,4. 4) it declares printf so the compiler knows how to call it. 5) a semicolon.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: forgetting the semicolon at the end of a statement, which the compiler rejects. Mistake: confusing = (assignment) with == (equality test) inside a condition. Exit: (a) What tool turns C source into an executable? (b) What value does main usually return on success? Answers: a compiler (such as clang); 0.

lessons.title: Algorithms and computational complexity
lessons.grammar_note: Big-O describes how running time grows as input size n grows, ignoring constant factors — O(n) and O(2n) are treated as the same class.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Compare linear and binary search, describe a couple of sorting algorithms, and rank running times with Big-O notation. Warm-up: to look up a name in a sorted phone book, would you flip page by page or open to the middle first?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure, and its efficiency matters as inputs grow. Linear search checks each item in turn, taking up to n steps — O(n). Binary search, on sorted data, checks the middle and throws away half the remaining range each step, taking about log2(n) steps — O(log n). Sorting matters because it unlocks fast search. Selection sort and bubble sort compare pairs and run in O(n^2), which is slow for big inputs. Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half, and merges them, running in O(n log n) — dramatically faster at scale. Big-O captures the worst-case growth rate and lets us reason about scale without timing a stopwatch.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Searching 1,000,000 sorted items: linear search may take up to 1,000,000 comparisons, but binary search takes about log2(1,000,000) which is roughly 20 — a huge difference. Ranking from fastest-growing-slowest to slowest: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2). A pseudocode linear search:

for each item in list:
    if item == target:
        return found
return not found

Worst case it inspects all n items. Binary search idea in pseudocode:

low = 0, high = n - 1
while low <= high:
    mid = (low + high) / 2
    if list[mid] == target: return found
    else if list[mid] < target: low = mid + 1
    else: high = mid - 1

Each loop halves the range, so it finishes in about log2(n) steps.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What is the Big-O of linear search? 2) What is the Big-O of binary search? 3) About how many steps does binary search need for 1024 sorted items? 4) Is O(n log n) faster or slower than O(n^2) for large n? 5) What must be true of the data before binary search works? Answers: 1) O(n). 2) O(log n). 3) log2(1024) = 10 steps. 4) faster. 5) it must be sorted.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: running binary search on unsorted data — halving only works when order is guaranteed. Mistake: reading O(2n) as worse than O(n); Big-O drops constant factors, so they are the same class. Exit: (a) Which sort runs in O(n log n): bubble sort or merge sort? (b) Which is faster for large n, O(log n) or O(n)? Answers: merge sort; O(log n).

questions.prompt: The binary number 1101 equals which decimal value?
How many distinct values can a single byte (8 bits) hold?
questions.explanation: 2^8 = 256 values, namely 0 through 255.

questions.prompt: Which function is the entry point of a C program?
questions.explanation: Execution begins in main.

questions.prompt: Linear search on a list of n items has which worst-case running time?
questions.explanation: It may inspect every one of the n items.

questions.prompt: Binary search requires the data to be…
questions.explanation: It discards half the range each step, which only works on sorted data.

questions.prompt: Merge sort runs in which time class?
questions.explanation: It splits, recursively sorts, and merges in O(n log n).

lessons.title: Arrays and strings
lessons.grammar_note: In C a string is an array of characters ending in a special null terminator, written '\0', which marks where the text stops.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Store many values of the same type in an array, index into it, and understand how C represents a string as characters in memory. Warm-up: in most programming languages, does the first element of an array sit at index 0 or index 1?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: An array is a contiguous block of memory holding several values of the same type, reachable by an index that starts at 0. Because the elements sit side by side, jumping to any index is instant. A string in C is simply an array of characters with a trailing null terminator '\0' so functions know where the text ends. That is why the word 'HI' needs three bytes, not two: 'H', 'I', and '\0'. Walking a string means looping until you reach that terminator, and computing its length means counting characters before it.

sections.heading: Worked examples
Your turn
sections.text: 1) What index holds the first element of an array? 2) In 'int a[4]', what is the largest valid index? 3) How many bytes does the C string "cat" occupy? 4) What character marks the end of a C string? 5) What does strlen("dog") return? Answers: 1) 0. 2) 3. 3) four — 'c','a','t','\0'. 4) the null terminator '\0'. 5) 3, the terminator is not counted.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: reading or writing one past the end of an array — index n in an array of size n does not exist. Mistake: forgetting the null terminator when sizing a string's storage. Exit: (a) At what index does the last element of 'int a[5]' live? (b) What extra character does a C string carry beyond its visible letters? Answers: index 4; the null terminator '\0'.

lessons.title: Functions and the call stack
lessons.grammar_note: A function's local variables and its return address live in a stack frame that is created on call and destroyed on return.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Write and call functions, pass arguments, return values, and explain how the call stack tracks which function is running. Warm-up: when function A calls function B, where does the program resume once B finishes?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A function is a named, reusable block that takes inputs (parameters), does work, and often returns a value. Functions let you decompose a hard problem into smaller pieces and avoid repeating code. When a function is called, the machine pushes a new stack frame holding that call's parameters, local variables, and the return address; when the function returns, its frame is popped and control resumes where it left off. Because frames stack up, a function can call another — even itself. A function that calls itself is recursive, and it must have a base case that stops the recursion, or the stack grows without end and overflows.

sections.heading: Worked examples
Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does a function push onto the stack when it is called? 2) What must every recursive function have to stop? 3) What does square(4) return given the code above? 4) When function B returns to function A, how does the machine know where to continue? 5) What is factorial(4)? Answers: 1) a stack frame (with its locals and return address). 2) a base case. 3) 16. 4) the return address stored in B's frame. 5) 24.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: writing recursion with no base case, which overflows the stack. Mistake: expecting changes to a passed-by-value argument to affect the caller's variable — C copies it into the new frame. Exit: (a) What data structure tracks active function calls? (b) What stops a recursive function from calling forever? Answers: the call stack; a base case.

lessons.title: Memory, pointers, and the stack and heap
lessons.grammar_note: A pointer holds a memory address; in C, &x gives the address of x and *p follows the pointer to the value it points at.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how memory is laid out, use pointers to read and write through addresses, and tell the stack apart from the heap. Warm-up: if a variable is a labeled box, what does a pointer store — the contents of the box or its location?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Memory is a long row of byte-sized cells, each with a numeric address. A pointer is a variable whose value is such an address. The operator & takes the address of a variable, and * dereferences a pointer to reach the value it points to. Memory is used in two main regions. The stack holds function frames and grows and shrinks automatically as calls come and go; its variables vanish when a function returns. The heap holds memory you request explicitly with malloc and keep until you free it, which is how programs build data that must outlive a single function. Forgetting to free heap memory causes a memory leak; using freed or never-allocated memory causes crashes.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
Address and dereference:

int x = 42;
int *p = &x;        // p holds the address of x
printf("%i\n", *p); // prints 42, the value at that address
*p = 7;             // writes through the pointer
printf("%i\n", x);  // now prints 7

Requesting heap memory:

int *arr = malloc(3 * sizeof(int));  // room for 3 ints on the heap
arr[0] = 10;
free(arr);                           // release it when done

The stack frame for a function disappears on return, but the heap block from malloc survives until free is called. That is why data meant to persist beyond one call belongs on the heap.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) What does a pointer store? 2) What does the & operator do in C? 3) What does *p give you? 4) Which region needs malloc and free: stack or heap? 5) What is a memory leak? Answers: 1) a memory address. 2) it gives the address of a variable. 3) the value stored at the address p holds. 4) the heap. 5) heap memory that is allocated but never freed, so it is lost until the program ends.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: dereferencing a pointer that was never pointed at valid memory, which crashes. Mistake: calling malloc but never free, leaking memory. Exit: (a) Which operator follows a pointer to its value? (b) Which memory region must be released manually? Answers: the * (dereference) operator; the heap (with free).

questions.prompt: In C, the first element of an array is at which index?
questions.explanation: Array indices start at 0.

questions.prompt: How many bytes does the C string "HI" occupy in memory?
questions.explanation: 'H', 'I', and the null terminator '\0' — three bytes.

questions.prompt: When a function is called, what is pushed onto the call stack?
options: a stack frame with locals and the return address
a pointer to the heap only
questions.explanation: Each call gets its own frame, popped when the function returns.

questions.prompt: Every recursive function needs which of these to terminate?
questions.explanation: The base case stops the recursion before the stack overflows.

questions.prompt: In C, what does the & operator do?
options: gives the address of a variable
questions.explanation: &x yields the memory address of x; * dereferences.

questions.prompt: Memory requested with malloc lives on the… and must be released with…
questions.explanation: malloc allocates on the heap; free releases it.

lessons.title: Data structures: linked lists, hash tables, and trees
lessons.grammar_note: A node is a small record that holds a value plus one or more pointers linking it to other nodes.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Describe how linked lists, hash tables, and binary search trees store data, and reason about the speed each one offers. Warm-up: an array must sit in one contiguous block; what lets a linked list grow without moving everything?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Different structures trade off speed, memory, and flexibility. A linked list chains nodes together, each node holding a value and a pointer to the next; it grows easily but you must walk from the front to reach an item, so lookup is O(n). A hash table stores each value in a bucket chosen by a hash function of its key, giving average O(1) insert and lookup — as long as the hash spreads keys evenly; when two keys collide in the same bucket, you chain them, which slows things down. A binary search tree keeps values ordered so that at each node everything smaller sits left and everything larger sits right; a balanced tree gives O(log n) search, but a badly shaped one can degrade toward O(n). Choosing a structure means matching its strengths to how you will read and write the data.

sections.heading: Worked examples
Your turn
sections.text: 1) What two things does a linked-list node hold? 2) What marks the end of a singly linked list? 3) What is the average lookup time of a good hash table? 4) In a binary search tree, do smaller values go left or right? 5) What happens in a hash table when two keys map to the same bucket? Answers: 1) a value and a pointer to the next node. 2) a NULL next pointer. 3) O(1). 4) left. 5) a collision, resolved by chaining the entries in that bucket.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: expecting O(1) lookup in a linked list — you must traverse from the head, which is O(n). Mistake: assuming a binary search tree stays fast even when built from already-sorted data, which can make it lopsided and slow. Exit: (a) Which structure offers average O(1) lookup? (b) What is the search time of a balanced binary search tree? Answers: a hash table; O(log n).

lessons.title: Moving to Python: higher-level abstraction
lessons.grammar_note: Python is interpreted and dynamically typed: you do not declare types or manage memory by hand, and indentation defines blocks instead of curly braces.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Translate familiar C ideas into Python, use its built-in lists and dictionaries, and explain what higher-level abstraction buys you. Warm-up: in C you sized strings and freed memory yourself; what part of that work does Python take over?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: Python raises the level of abstraction. It is interpreted rather than compiled, so you run source directly. It is dynamically typed, so a variable takes whatever type you assign without a declaration. It manages memory automatically, so there is no malloc or free. Blocks are marked by indentation, not braces. Common structures come built in: a list is a resizable array, and a dictionary is a hash table with friendly syntax. You write far less code for the same task, trading some low-level control and raw speed for clarity and speed of development. Everything you learned about algorithms and data structures still applies — Python just hides the plumbing.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
The greeting and a loop, now in Python:

print("hello, world")

for i in range(3):
    print(i)          # prints 0, 1, 2

A list and a dictionary:

scores = [90, 80, 70]
print(scores[0])       # 90
scores.append(60)      # grows automatically

ages = {"alice": 30, "bob": 25}
print(ages["alice"])   # 30, an average O(1) lookup

A function, with no type declarations:

def square(x):
    return x * x

print(square(5))       # 25

Notice there is no sizing, no null terminator, and no free — Python handles memory and growth for you.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Is Python compiled ahead of time or interpreted? 2) What defines a block in Python instead of braces? 3) Which built-in type is Python's hash table? 4) Does Python require you to call free? 5) What does range(3) produce for a loop? Answers: 1) interpreted. 2) indentation. 3) the dictionary (dict). 4) no, memory is managed automatically. 5) the values 0, 1, 2.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: mixing tabs and spaces so Python's indentation-based blocks break. Mistake: assuming a Python list and a C array behave identically — the Python list resizes itself and holds any types. Exit: (a) What replaces manual memory management from C? (b) What Python type plays the role of a hash table? Answers: automatic memory management (garbage collection); the dictionary.

lessons.title: SQL and storing data
lessons.grammar_note: SQL keywords are conventionally written in uppercase and each statement ends with a semicolon; a WHERE clause filters which rows an operation touches.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Model data as tables and read, insert, update, and delete rows with the four core SQL statements. Warm-up: a program's variables vanish when it exits; what do you need so data survives between runs?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A relational database stores data in tables — rows are records and columns are fields, each with a type. This lets data persist on disk and be queried efficiently, often with an index for fast lookup. Four statements do most of the work: SELECT reads rows, INSERT adds them, UPDATE changes them, and DELETE removes them. A WHERE clause restricts which rows are affected, so it is essential for UPDATE and DELETE. Because tables can reference each other by a shared key, you can relate data across tables — for example linking an order to the customer who placed it. SQL is a declarative language: you describe what rows you want, and the database figures out how to fetch them.

sections.heading: Worked examples
Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which statement reads rows from a table? 2) Which statement adds a new row? 3) What does a WHERE clause do? 4) What is dangerous about 'DELETE FROM users;' with no WHERE? 5) Write SQL to select the name column of everyone in the users table. Answers: 1) SELECT. 2) INSERT. 3) it filters which rows the statement affects. 4) it deletes every row in the table. 5) SELECT name FROM users;

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: running UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause, which changes or removes every row. Mistake: expecting SELECT to change data — it only reads. Exit: (a) Which statement changes existing rows? (b) Which clause limits which rows are affected? Answers: UPDATE; the WHERE clause.

lessons.title: Web basics: HTTP, HTML, CSS, and a dynamic app
lessons.grammar_note:
HTML structures content with tags such as

and

, CSS styles that content, and HTTP is the request-and-response protocol carrying it between browser and server.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Explain how a browser and server talk over HTTP, mark up a page with HTML, style it with CSS, and describe what makes an app dynamic. Warm-up: when you type an address and press enter, what does your browser send to the server?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: The web runs on requests and responses. A browser sends an HTTP request (commonly GET to fetch a page or POST to submit data) to a server, which replies with an HTTP response carrying a status code and content. Status codes summarize the outcome: 200 means success, 302 a redirect, 404 not found, and 500 a server error. The content is usually HTML, a language of nested tags that gives a page structure — headings, paragraphs, links, forms. CSS then styles that structure, controlling color, layout, and fonts. A static site returns the same fixed files to everyone. A dynamic app runs code on the server that builds the response on the fly — often reading or writing a database with SQL — so different users can see different, up-to-date content. That server code ties together everything in this course: logic, data structures, and storage.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text:
A small HTML page: My Page

Hello

Welcome to my site.

Tags nest: contains a heading

and a paragraph

. A dash of CSS to color the heading: h1 { color: blue; text-align: center; } Dynamic behavior in words: a browser sends GET /profile; the server runs code that issues SELECT name FROM users WHERE id = 42, drops the result into an HTML template, and returns a 200 response with a page personalized for that user. Change the user, change the page — that is what 'dynamic' means.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: 1) Which HTTP method typically fetches a page? 2) What does status code 404 mean? 3) What is HTML responsible for on a page? 4) What is CSS responsible for? 5) What makes an app dynamic rather than static? Answers: 1) GET. 2) not found. 3) the structure and content (via tags). 4) the styling and layout. 5) server code builds each response at request time, often from a database, instead of serving the same fixed file.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: confusing HTML's job (structure) with CSS's job (style). Mistake: assuming a 200 status guarantees the content is what you wanted — it only means the request succeeded. Exit: (a) What protocol carries requests and responses on the web? (b) Which status code means success? Answers: HTTP; 200.

questions.prompt: A good hash table provides average lookup time of…
questions.explanation: A well-spread hash function makes lookup roughly constant time.

questions.prompt: In a binary search tree, values smaller than a node are found…
questions.explanation: Smaller left, larger right — that ordering enables O(log n) search when balanced.

questions.prompt: Compared with C, Python handles memory by…
questions.explanation: Python manages memory automatically; there is no manual malloc or free.

questions.prompt: Which SQL statement changes existing rows?
questions.explanation: UPDATE modifies rows, usually narrowed by a WHERE clause.

questions.prompt: Which HTTP status code means 'not found'?
questions.explanation: 404 signals the requested resource was not found.

questions.prompt: On a web page, CSS is responsible for…
questions.explanation: HTML gives structure; CSS controls color, layout, and fonts.

lessons.title: Capstone: planning your final project
lessons.grammar_note: A good project scope is small enough to finish and clear enough that you can list, before you start, exactly what 'done' looks like.

sections.heading: What you'll be able to do
sections.text: Turn a vague idea into a concrete, buildable final project with a defined scope, a chosen tech stack, a data model, and a plan of milestones. Warm-up: which topic from this course excited you most — could it become the heart of a small program?

sections.heading: The idea
sections.text: A final project is where the separate pieces of this course combine into something you build end to end. The hardest part is not coding but scoping: picking a problem small enough to finish yet meaty enough to be worth doing. A workable plan answers a few questions in order. What problem does this solve, and for whom? What is the minimum version that would count as working — the smallest thing that delivers value? Which tools fit: a C or Python program, a database with SQL, a web front end of HTML and CSS, or some combination? What data will you store, and in what tables? Finally, break the build into milestones so you always have a next small step and can tell how far along you are. Plan first, then build; a clear plan turns a daunting project into a sequence of manageable tasks.

sections.heading: Worked examples
sections.text: Example plan for a personal reading tracker. Problem: I keep losing track of which books I have read and want to read. Users: just me, to start. Minimum version: add a book, mark it read or unread, and list all books. Stack: a small web app with HTML and CSS for the pages, server code in Python for the logic, and SQL for storage. Data model: a single table books(id, title, author, status). Milestones: (1) create the database table; (2) list existing books on a page; (3) add a form that INSERTs a new book; (4) let a click UPDATE a book's status to read; (5) style the page with CSS. Each milestone is a self-contained, testable step, and after any one of them you still have something that runs.

sections.heading: Your turn
sections.text: Sketch a plan for a project of your own by answering these. 1) What problem does it solve, in one sentence? 2) Who is the user? 3) What is the minimum working version? 4) Which parts of the stack (C, Python, SQL, HTML/CSS) will you use? 5) What tables and columns will store your data? 6) List three milestones in order. Sample answers for a to-do app: 1) helps me remember tasks. 2) me. 3) add a task, list tasks, mark one done. 4) Python plus SQL, with HTML and CSS pages. 5) tasks(id, description, done). 6) create the table; show the task list; add a form to INSERT a task.

sections.heading: Common mistakes & exit ticket
sections.text: Mistake: scoping too big, so nothing ships — start from the minimum working version and add from there. Mistake: coding before deciding what data you will store, which forces painful rewrites. Exit: (a) What should you define before writing any code? (b) Why break the build into milestones? Answers: the scope, including the minimum working version and the data model; so you always have a small, testable next step and can measure progress.

questions.prompt: The binary number 1010 equals which decimal value?
ASCII assigns each character a number using how much storage per character?
questions.explanation: ASCII uses one byte per character; Unicode extends this to cover all scripts.

questions.prompt: What does a compiler like clang do to a C program?
options: translates the source into machine code before running
questions.explanation: It compiles the whole source into an executable ahead of time.

questions.prompt: In C, a string is stored as an array of characters ending in…
questions.explanation: The '\0' marks where the text ends.

questions.prompt: When a function is called, the machine pushes onto the stack a…
options: stack frame with locals and a return address
questions.explanation: Each call gets a frame, popped when the function returns.

questions.prompt: In C, the * operator applied to a pointer does what?
options: dereferences it to reach the value it points to
questions.explanation: * follows the pointer to the value; & takes an address.

questions.prompt: Memory allocated with malloc must eventually be released with…
questions.explanation: free releases heap memory; failing to call it causes a leak.

questions.prompt: Which structure offers average O(1) insertion and lookup?
questions.explanation: A hash table maps keys to buckets for roughly constant-time access.

questions.prompt: Compared with C, Python is…
options: interpreted and dynamically typed with automatic memory management
questions.explanation: Python runs interpreted, infers types, and manages memory for you.

questions.prompt: Which SQL statement reads rows without changing them?
questions.explanation: SELECT only reads; the others modify data.

questions.prompt: On the web, HTML provides structure and CSS provides…
questions.explanation: CSS controls color, layout, and fonts atop HTML's structure.
